unit.name: Key Developments in Film and Film Technology
unit.subtitle: From the Lumiere brothers to IMAX and iPhones: the technologies that changed what a film can be.

lessons.title: Silent Cinema to Sound: 1895-1935
lessons.description: From the Lumiere brothers' first screening to Technicolor: how cinema found its voice.
lessons.content_html:
The Birth of Moving Images: 1895

On 28 December 1895, Auguste and Louis Lumière projected a series of short films to a paying audience in the basement of the Grand Café in Paris. The films lasted less than a minute each and showed simple scenes: workers leaving a factory, a train pulling into a station, a gardener being sprayed with water. There was no story, no intertitles, no sound beyond the projector’s rattle — yet audiences reportedly flinched when the locomotive approached. Cinema had arrived.

The Lumière brothers used their own invention, the Cinématographe, which could both record and project moving images. Unlike Thomas Edison’s Kinetoscope — a single-viewer peep-show device — the Cinématographe projected onto a screen for a crowd, establishing cinema as a collective, public experience from the very beginning.

Key Fact

The Lumière brothers held the first public film screening on 28 December 1895 in Paris, using the Cinématographe. Cinema was born as a shared public spectacle, not a private entertainment.

Silent Film and the Grammar of Cinema

Between 1895 and the late 1920s, cinema was silent — or rather, it was never completely silent, since live piano, organ or full orchestra accompanied most screenings. What it lacked was synchronised recorded sound. Filmmakers compensated through increasingly sophisticated visual storytelling: longer films, more complex narratives, and a rapidly developing language of editing and mise-en-scène.

D.W. Griffith, directing in the United States in the 1910s, helped codify many of the editing techniques that remain standard today: the close-up to convey emotion, cross-cutting between simultaneous events to build tension, and the tracking shot following a character through space. Whatever the moral problems with his most famous work, his technical influence on how stories are told through pictures was vast.

In Soviet Russia during the 1920s, Sergei Eisenstein developed a different approach to editing. Where Hollywood’s continuity editing aimed to make cuts invisible, Eisenstein’s theory of montage treated the cut as a collision: juxtapose a close-up of a dead horse with a shot of workers, and the audience feels something beyond what either image contains. Eisenstein’s influence is still visible in modern political films and advertising.

Silent films used intertitles — printed text cards cut into the action — to convey dialogue and key narrative information. Skilled directors minimised them: a film relying on intertitles every thirty seconds was thought clumsy; the best silent cinema told its story primarily through image and performance. Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, and Lon Chaney built entire emotional performances visible in their bodies and faces rather than in speech, a discipline that remains a benchmark for expressive acting technique.

The limitation of silence also pushed filmmakers towards exaggerated gesture and lighting. High-contrast chiaroscuro lighting — borrowed from Expressionist painting and German cinema — communicated mood that dialogue would otherwise carry. The Expressionist films of the early 1920s (heavily shadowed sets, distorted architecture, extreme angles) represent one of the purest achievements of what silent cinema could do that sound cinema would later partly lose.

The Rise of Hollywood and the Studio System

By the early 1920s, Los Angeles had become the centre of world film production. The Californian light, the variety of landscapes, and the distance from the eastern patent trusts that controlled early cinema equipment all contributed. A handful of large studios — MGM, Paramount, Warner Bros., RKO and Fox — came to dominate production, distribution and exhibition. They owned the theatres as well as the films, and they employed actors, directors and technicians on exclusive long-term contracts. This industrial model shaped what kind of stories were told and how reliably they could be told at scale.

Understanding the studio system is not just historical detail — it explains why Hollywood films of the 1930s–50s look, sound and feel the way they do. The studios had house styles, preferred genres and star personalities built into their production processes. When you study any US film from this era, its institutional context — which studio made it, what genre it belongs to, which stars were under contract — is part of what produced it. AO1 (knowledge and understanding) credit comes from being able to anchor a film to its institutional moment; AO2 (analyse and apply) credit comes from using that context to explain specific filmic choices.

The Jazz Singer and Synchronised Sound: 1927

On 6 October 1927, Warner Bros. released The Jazz Singer, starring Al Jolson. It was not the first film to have recorded sound (Warner had experimented with Vitaphone sound-on-disc technology since 1926), but it was the first feature-length sound film to achieve mass commercial success. Jolson’s spoken improvisation — a brief aside to the orchestra before a song — announced to audiences that cinema had changed. The era of “talkies” had arrived.

The transition to synchronised sound was rapid but not painless. Camera technology that had become wonderfully mobile during the silent era suddenly had to retreat: early sound cameras were enclosed in heavy, sound-proof “blimps” to prevent the camera’s mechanical noise from appearing on the soundtrack. Microphones had to be hidden on set. For several years in the late 1920s and early 1930s, films became visually more static as directors adapted to the new constraints. The camerawork of the late silent era — free, expressive, kinetic — would take years to recover.

Key Fact

The Jazz Singer (1927, Warner Bros.) used the Vitaphone sound-on-disc system to become the first commercially successful feature-length sound film. The transition to “talkies” transformed the industry within three years.

Three-Strip Technicolor: 1935

Colour processes had existed since the earliest days of cinema: hand-tinting individual frames, two-colour processes, and various dye methods all pre-date the most significant advance. In 1935, Rouben Mamoulian directed Becky Sharp, the first feature film shot in the full three-strip Technicolor process. Three-strip Technicolor used a specially built camera that simultaneously exposed three separate strips of film, each recording one of the three primary colours of light. The results were rich, saturated and immediately recognisable — the gleaming reds and greens of Gone with the Wind (1939) and The Wizard of Oz (1939) are its most celebrated early examples.

Technicolor carried significant institutional constraints alongside its visual rewards. The process required a specialised camera, which the Technicolor Corporation rented (not sold) to studios, and it required Technicolor’s own colour consultants on set. The process was expensive and slow. This meant that early Technicolor films were typically large-scale prestige productions or musicals — subjects where the visual spectacle could justify the cost. Intimate, low-budget dramas remained in black and white for decades.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on key developments in film technology typically ask you to “identify”, “name” or “explain the effect of” a specific development. The most common error is giving the right information but the wrong date or attaching it to the wrong film. Precision matters here: Vitaphone was the synchronised sound system used in The Jazz Singer (1927) — not simply “colour” or “widescreen”. For “explain the effect” questions, do not just describe the technology — say what it changed for filmmakers or audiences. For example, synchronised sound changed what actors could do on screen (authentic dialogue became possible) but also constrained what cameras could do (heavy blimps limited movement). That cause-and-consequence structure is what an “explain the effect” answer needs.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Lumière brothers’ first public screening in Paris on 28 December 1895 established cinema as a collective, public experience. Their Cinématographe projected film onto a screen for a crowd, setting the template for commercial cinema.
  • The Jazz Singer (1927, Warner Bros., Vitaphone) brought synchronised sound to commercial cinema. The transition to “talkies” briefly limited camera mobility but permanently transformed performance, dialogue and storytelling.
  • Becky Sharp (1935) was the first feature shot in three-strip Technicolor, enabling rich, saturated colour — but the process was expensive and institutionally controlled, limiting early colour cinema to prestige productions and musicals.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the development of Eisenstein's montage technique differed from Hollywood's approach to continuity editing. In your answer, explain what each technique does and what effect it creates for the spectator.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise account of both techniques, with a clear explanation of the difference in editorial philosophy. Continuity editing is identified as aiming to make cuts invisible, preserving coherent time and space and guiding the spectator smoothly through narrative. Montage is explained as a deliberate collision of contrasting images designed to produce an idea or emotion beyond either shot. The spectator's experience of each is specifically addressed: continuity editing creates immersion and identifies with characters; montage creates an intellectual and emotional impact through juxtaposition. Appropriate examples are used (e.g. Griffith's cross-cutting, Eisenstein's image-collision sequences). Specialist vocabulary is precise and sustained throughout.
Secure: Both techniques are explained and the key difference is identified. At least one effect on the spectator is stated. Some specialist vocabulary is used.
Developing: One technique is explained more fully than the other, or the difference is recognised without the spectator-effect being articulated. Vocabulary is present but may be imprecise.
Emerging: Basic description of one technique only, with little or no explanation of effect. Descriptive rather than analytical.

lessons.title: Widescreen, Steadicam and the Push for Spectacle: 1948-1990s
lessons.description: How the Paramount decree, widescreen formats, Steadicam and early CGI reshaped cinema.
lessons.content_html:
The Paramount Decree and the End of the Studio System: 1948

In 1948, the United States Supreme Court ruled in United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc. that the major Hollywood studios had illegally monopolised the film industry. The studios had operated a vertically integrated system: they produced films, distributed them and owned the theatres where audiences watched them. The court decision — known as the Paramount decree — forced the studios to divest their cinema chains. Without guaranteed screen access, studios could no longer be certain of a return on every film they made. The comfortable industrial certainties of the studio system began to erode.

The Paramount decree coincided with a second existential threat: the arrival of television in American homes. By the early 1950s, millions of households had a small screen in the living room that provided free entertainment. Cinema attendances fell sharply. The studios responded with a technological strategy: give audiences something their television set could never offer. The answer was spectacle — bigger, wider, louder, more immersive.

Key Fact

The 1948 Paramount decree forced Hollywood studios to sell off their cinema chains, ending vertical integration. Combined with the rise of television, it pushed studios towards spectacular widescreen technologies to draw audiences back to cinemas.

Widescreen Formats: CinemaScope and the 1950s Revolution

The most visible technological response to television was the widescreen format. Standard cinema of the 1930s and 1940s used an aspect ratio of approximately 1.37:1 — a near-square frame not much wider than a television screen. In 1953, 20th Century Fox introduced CinemaScope, using an anamorphic lens system to squeeze a panoramic image onto standard 35mm film. The resulting ratio — approximately 2.55:1 — was nearly twice as wide as the television image and completely transformed how directors composed their shots.

Paramount’s rival process, VistaVision, used a different approach: running the film horizontally through the camera rather than vertically, doubling the area of each frame and producing exceptional sharpness. Other studios experimented with three-projector systems (Cinerama) and even 3D processes that required audiences to wear polarised glasses. Most of these formats proved too complex or expensive to sustain; CinemaScope and similar anamorphic processes dominated the widescreen era and still inform the standard theatrical aspect ratios used today.

A wide frame is not simply a bigger frame — it is a different compositional challenge. In a near-square frame, the director controls where the eye goes by placing the subject centrally; the sides of the frame are relatively empty. In a widescreen frame, the sides become active: two characters can be held in genuine spatial tension at opposite edges, or the environment can dwarf the human figure in ways that carry thematic weight. Early critics complained that CinemaScope was only suited to “snakes and funerals” — things that are naturally horizontal. Over time, directors learned to activate the full width of the frame for intimate drama as well as epic spectacle. This shift in compositional thinking is directly relevant to your analysis of framing in any film made after the mid-1950s.

Lightweight Cameras and the French New Wave

The 1950s and 1960s also saw the development of smaller, lighter cameras that could be carried on the shoulder and operated without a tripod or dolly. Handheld cinematography had been pioneered in documentary work, where the ability to follow events without setting up heavy equipment was essential. In the late 1950s, a group of young French directors — including Jean-Luc Godard and François Truffaut — adopted documentary aesthetics deliberately in fiction films, rejecting the polished studio look in favour of location shooting, natural light and a camera that moved impulsively with the action. The resulting films felt urgent, alive and deliberately rough-edged in a way that studio filmmaking could not replicate.

The French New Wave influence spread across cinema worldwide in the 1960s and 1970s. The shaky, spontaneous handheld image became associated with psychological realism and documentary authenticity, a connotation it retains today. The camera no longer needed to be a fixed, authoritative observer; it could be implicated in the action, uncertain, reactive — a participant rather than a recorder.

Key Fact

The Steadicam was invented by Garrett Brown and first used on a major production in 1975–1976 (notably on Rocky and Bound for Glory in 1976). It allowed cameras to move fluidly through space without the jerkiness of handheld work or the constraint of tracks and dollies.

The Steadicam: Garrett Brown and the Floating Camera

In 1975, American inventor and cameraman Garrett Brown developed the Steadicam, a body-mounted stabilisation system that used a counterbalanced arm to isolate the camera from the operator’s movements. The Steadicam could follow an actor through a door, up a staircase, around a corner, into a crowd — all in one continuous shot — while the image remained perfectly smooth. It combined the freedom of handheld work with the visual composure of a dolly shot.

The Steadicam’s effect on filmmaking was immediate. Stanley Kubrick used it extensively in The Shining (1980) to track a child on a tricycle along hotel corridors: the camera glided behind him at precisely his height, following with an uncanny, unhurried smoothness that felt neither like a tracking dolly (which would be mechanical and distant) nor a handheld camera (which would feel urgent and human). The sensation was of something inhuman, patient and predatory — a feeling produced entirely by the specific technology of the Steadicam applied with deliberate intent. This is the kind of link between micro-choice (camera stabilisation system) and macro-meaning (psychological dread, threat) that strong film analysis requires.

Early CGI: Industrial Light and Magic, Terminator 2 and Jurassic Park

George Lucas founded Industrial Light & Magic (ILM) in 1975 to produce the effects for Star Wars (1977). Whilst Star Wars relied primarily on physical models, optical printing and practical effects rather than digital imagery, ILM became the leading centre for the development of computer-generated imagery (CGI) over the following decade. Two films marked the tipping points of practical possibility.

In Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991, directed by James Cameron), the T-1000 antagonist was rendered as a liquid-metal shape-shifter: its surface rippled, reformed, and mimicked other surfaces. The sequence in which it reforms from a puddle of mercury — beginning with a flat, reflective pool on the floor, then gathering into a standing figure, its surface resolving from abstract silver to the face and uniform of a police officer — demonstrated that CGI could now create convincing organic movement in a way no physical effect could match. In Jurassic Park (1993, directed by Steven Spielberg), CGI dinosaurs were integrated with live-action photography in extended wide shots: a herd of herbivores stampeding across a sunlit valley, the animals casting shadows on real ground, their legs moving in the dust. The integration was seamless enough that audiences understood they were watching something that could not be filmed because it did not exist. Both films used compositing techniques to embed generated images within photographed environments.

A common error is to credit the Steadicam to a studio (often Panavision or ILM) rather than to its actual inventor. The Steadicam was developed by Garrett Brown, an independent inventor and camera operator. Brown patented the device and licensed it to the industry — it was not developed inside a studio’s R&D department. Knowing the inventor’s name is important: exam questions specifically ask for Garrett Brown, not a corporate name.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For “identify” or “name” questions on this topic, precision is everything. Students often confuse CinemaScope (1953, 20th Century Fox) with the Paramount decree (1948) — these are different developments, different years, different studios. Similarly, the Steadicam was invented by Garrett Brown in 1975 — not by a studio or by ILM. For “explain the effect” questions, always state the consequence for filmmakers or audiences, not just the fact of the technology. For example: “The Steadicam allowed directors to create smooth continuous tracking shots through complex spaces without rails or dollies, enabling a new kind of psychological effect that neither pure handheld nor pure dolly work could produce.” That final clause — what it could do that other methods could not — is what earns the effect marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1948 Paramount decree ended vertical integration in Hollywood, forcing studios to sell their cinema chains. Combined with the television threat, it drove a wave of technological spectacle in the 1950s — widescreen formats, 3D, colour — designed to offer audiences something their home screens could not.
  • The Steadicam, invented by Garrett Brown in 1975, transformed camera movement by combining the fluidity of a dolly shot with the freedom of handheld work. Its most celebrated use — Kubrick’s The Shining (1980) — demonstrates how a specific camera technology can produce macro-level psychological effects.
  • Early CGI milestones — Terminator 2 (1991) and Jurassic Park (1993) — demonstrated that computer-generated imagery could be composited seamlessly into live action, opening possibilities for storytelling that practical effects could not achieve.

lessons.title: Digital, Streaming and Citizen Cinema: 1995-2018
lessons.description: Toy Story, iPhone filmmaking, Netflix and IMAX: how digital technology democratised cinema.
lessons.content_html:
Toy Story and the First Computer-Generated Feature: 1995

In 1995, Pixar Animation Studios released Toy Story, the world’s first feature-length film made entirely with computer-generated animation. Directed by John Lasseter and co-produced with Disney, the film ran for 77 minutes and was generated entirely by computers — no hand-drawn frames, no physical sets, no photographed actors. Every surface, shadow, and movement was calculated by software. The film was a commercial and critical success, and it announced a new era in animated filmmaking.

A critical distinction is worth fixing in memory here: Toy Story was not the first film to use computer-generated imagery. Live-action films had been incorporating CGI elements since the 1980s, and significant milestones — the Terminator 2 and Jurassic Park achievements of the early 1990s — preceded it. What made Toy Story historically significant was that it was the first feature-length film composed entirely of computer-generated images, with no photography involved in the image-making. This distinction matters: exam questions specifically ask about the “first computer-generated feature”, not the “first film with CGI”.

Key Fact

Toy Story (1995), directed by John Lasseter at Pixar Animation Studios (co-produced with Disney), was the world’s first feature-length computer-generated animated film. It was not the first film with CGI, but the first feature composed entirely of computer-generated images.

Digital Cinematography and the DV Revolution

Alongside the rise of computer animation, the 1990s and 2000s brought a revolution in how live-action films were captured. Film stock — celluloid — had been the standard recording medium since cinema’s earliest days. It was expensive to buy, expensive to process, and limited in quantity: a director had a finite number of takes before the cost became prohibitive. Digital cinematography changed this calculation fundamentally. Digital sensors recorded to memory cards or hard drives; footage could be reviewed immediately on set; takes were essentially free. This changed the economics and culture of production.

Consumer-grade digital video (DV) cameras also began to appear in the late 1990s: small, lightweight, affordable, and capable of producing images that could be broadcast or projected. The “DV revolution” made it possible for filmmakers without studio budgets or studio equipment to produce feature-length work. Directors such as Lars von Trier used consumer DV cameras deliberately, as an aesthetic and political statement about cinema’s relationship to expensive technology. The rough, video-like quality of DV footage — its specific colour response, its softness, its visible grain in low light — became a recognisable aesthetic in independent filmmaking of the late 1990s and 2000s.

Citizen Filmmaking: Tangerine and the Smartphone

By the 2010s, smartphone cameras had reached a quality that made serious filmmaking possible on a device that fits in a pocket. The landmark moment in mainstream cinema came in 2015 with Tangerine, directed by Sean Baker. The film was shot entirely on an iPhone 5S using the Filmic Pro app and anamorphic lenses attached to the phone. It premiered at the Sundance Film Festival and received wide critical acclaim, demonstrating that a compelling, professional-quality narrative feature could be made for a fraction of the cost of conventional film production.

Tangerine’s visual approach was partly a consequence of its shooting method. The iPhone’s wide-angle lens naturally produced a specific look: faces often filled much of the frame, backgrounds fell away into soft-focus colour, and the camera could move through the bustle of Los Angeles streets with an immediacy that a conventional film camera rig could not match. The film’s energy and intimacy were inseparable from the technology used to make it. This is a key principle: technology does not just determine what is possible; it shapes the aesthetic character of what is made.

The phrase “democratisation of production” refers to the way that digital and smartphone technology reduced the cost barrier to making films. In the era of celluloid, a feature-length film required expensive film stock, laboratory processing and specialist camera equipment — barriers that effectively restricted filmmaking to those with institutional backing. Digital cameras, editing software and smartphone devices removed most of those barriers. Anyone with a phone and a free editing app can now shoot and distribute a short film. The question this raises — relevant for Film Studies at any level — is what this means for whose stories get told and which voices get heard. Films like Tangerine told stories about communities (transgender sex workers in Los Angeles) that the Hollywood studio system had historically ignored, using equipment that the studio system would never have sanctioned.

Netflix and the Streaming Revolution

Netflix was founded in 1997 as a postal DVD rental service. In 2007, it launched its online streaming service, initially for a small catalogue of titles. Growth was rapid. By 2013 Netflix was producing its own original content; by 2016 it had over 80 million subscribers globally. The tipping point came in 2017 when streaming overtook DVD as the primary distribution method for film and television content in the United States. Physical media — the disc in the box on the shelf — had been the dominant home-viewing format since the 1980s; within a decade of Netflix’s streaming launch, it was secondary.

The implications for cinema were profound. Films could reach global audiences without a theatrical release; directors who might not have attracted studio backing found Netflix willing to fund adventurous projects. The traditional window between theatrical release and home viewing, which had been several months, compressed dramatically — and with the Covid-19 pandemic of 2020 closed cinemas worldwide, some major releases went directly to streaming. For audiences, streaming meant access to an enormous catalogue on demand, at home, without scheduling. For the film industry, it raised questions about what “cinema” means when most viewers watch films on a laptop or phone screen.

Key Fact

Netflix launched its streaming service in 2007. By 2017, streaming had overtaken DVD as the primary distribution format for film and television content in the United States, fundamentally changing how audiences accessed cinema.

IMAX and the Blockbuster Spectacle: Avengers: Infinity War (2018)

At the same time as smartphone cinema was making production cheaper and more accessible, the premium end of filmmaking was pushing in the opposite direction: towards the largest, highest-resolution cameras ever used in mainstream fiction production. The IMAX format had been used in documentary and nature films since the 1970s and in partial sequences of mainstream releases from the early 2000s. In 2018, Avengers: Infinity War, directed by Anthony and Joe Russo, became the first major fiction feature to be shot entirely on IMAX cameras. Every frame was captured at the maximum resolution available, producing an image quality that could fill a six-storey screen with detail visible to the last row of the auditorium. The film was designed to be a theatrical event — an argument that cinema in a premium auditorium offers an experience categorically different from anything available at home.

Many students write that a film was “shown in IMAX” and think this is the same as saying it was “shot on IMAX cameras”. These are completely different things. Most films shown in IMAX cinemas are standard productions digitally upscaled for the large screen — the IMAX branding refers to the presentation format, not the capture format. Avengers: Infinity War (2018) was historically significant because it was the first major fiction feature shot entirely using IMAX cameras during production. The difference in image quality between footage shot on IMAX cameras and footage upscaled for IMAX projection is substantial. Do not conflate the two in exam answers.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most frequent error on this topic is confusing Toy Story (1995) — the first feature-length computer-generated film — with the first film to use CGI. CGI appeared in live-action films earlier in the 1990s; Toy Story was the first entirely computer-generated feature. Similarly, many students write “IMAX” when they mean “shot entirely on IMAX cameras” — these are different things, and the exam will test the distinction. For “explain the effect” questions, the key move is to state what the technology changed for filmmakers or audiences. The democratisation of production question invites you to say: cheaper digital technology made it possible for directors outside the studio system to tell stories that would otherwise not have been made. Give a specific example: Tangerine (2015), Sean Baker, iPhone 5S.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Toy Story (1995, Pixar/Disney, directed by John Lasseter) was the world’s first feature-length computer-generated animated film — not the first film with CGI, but the first feature made entirely without photography.
  • Digital and smartphone technology democratised film production: Tangerine (2015, Sean Baker) was shot on an iPhone 5S, demonstrating that low-cost tools could produce professional, acclaimed narrative cinema and tell stories the studio system ignored.
  • Netflix launched streaming in 2007; by 2017 it had overtaken DVD as the primary distribution format. Meanwhile, Avengers: Infinity War (2018) became the first major fiction feature shot entirely on IMAX cameras — the highest and lowest cost ends of the industry developing in parallel.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the development of smartphone filmmaking, as demonstrated by Tangerine (2015), changed what kinds of stories cinema could tell and whose stories were told.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The answer explains what Tangerine demonstrated technically (shot entirely on iPhone 5S with anamorphic lens adaptor; Filmic Pro app) and articulates how the technology shaped the aesthetic (close framing, immediacy, soft-focus backgrounds). The answer then makes the macro-level argument: the low cost and mobility of smartphone cameras enabled directors without studio budgets to make work about communities and stories that the traditional studio system's financial logic had excluded. Tangerine's subject matter (transgender sex workers in Los Angeles) is identified as an example of a story that found a form of production suited to its scale and community. The link between technology (micro: specific camera choice, specific visual properties) and institutional/representational consequence (macro: democratisation, diversification of whose stories are told) is explicit and sustained. Specialist vocabulary is precise throughout.
Secure: The technological facts are correct and the main point about democratisation is made. Some link between the specific camera and its aesthetic effect is present. Subject matter of Tangerine is referenced.
Developing: The film is correctly identified as shot on an iPhone but analysis of the aesthetic or representational consequence is thin. Vocabulary is present but imprecise.
Emerging: Basic correct identification of the film with little or no analysis of effect on storytelling or representation.

glossary_terms.definition: A film made entirely from images generated by computer software, with no live-action photography; distinct from films that merely incorporate CGI elements alongside photographed footage.
A method of capturing moving images directly onto electronic storage as digital data rather than onto photographic film, removing the per-foot cost of film stock.
The process by which falling costs and widening access to production technology make filmmaking available to people and communities who were previously excluded by the high cost of equipment.
A method of delivering film and television content over the internet directly to the viewer's device, without downloading the file and without the need for physical media such as DVD or Blu-ray.
A large-format film and digital camera and projection system producing images significantly larger and sharper than standard 35mm film, used for a premium theatrical experience.
Light-sensitive plastic film coated with chemical emulsion, used as the recording medium for cinema from its earliest days until the digital era.
